cards.title: Assign cross-functional store ownership before choosing the first hire
cards.summary: The administrator owns contracts, partnerships, strategy, reporting and brand image, and a founder can fill this seat alone until revenue supports a hire.
cards.use_when: Deciding who your first operational hire should be when launching a new store or formalising an unstructured one-person operation.
steps: Write the administrator's scope before hiring: overseeing buying contracts, managing supplier and partner relationships, reporting, strategy creation, and owning brand image.
If budget is tight, act as the administrator yourself and personally cover the core tasks in the other silos rather than hiring a generalist who does none of them well.
Once revenue and order volume make the workload unmanageable (the source does not give a number), hire into the role instead of continuing to personally absorb it.
Keep reporting in this role so one person can see the full operation — sales, spend and fulfillment status — and can make trade-off decisions across silos.
When hiring, screen for the ability to coordinate across customer service, fulfillment, marketing and development, since this role's value is cross-functional oversight.
Verify current hiring market expectations and any contractor/employment classification rules for your jurisdiction before posting.
caveats: This is a single practitioner's recommended structure, not a proven org chart; very small stores often run flat with the founder doing everything indefinitely.
cards.source_name: How to Build an E-commerce Team from Scratch.docx

cards.title: Staff customer service to clear purchase hesitation
cards.summary: Confused shoppers do not buy, so a customer service function should exist to answer questions and remove friction right before checkout.
cards.use_when: Designing your pre-purchase support coverage, chat/email staffing or FAQ operation to raise PDP and cart conversion.
steps: Treat customer service as a conversion function, not a cost center: its job is to answer buyer questions so they proceed to enter payment details.

Identify the recurring confusions that block purchase (sizing, shipping time, returns, ingredient/material questions) by reviewing incoming messages, and answer them on the product page itself so fewer people need to ask.
Staff enough response coverage for the hours your traffic actually converts in, since unanswered pre-purchase questions are lost orders.
Write response templates for the top question types so answers are fast and consistent, but allow staff to handle unusual cases individually.
Feed the question themes back to marketing and web development — repeated questions point to copy or navigation failures, not to bad customers.
Measure pre-purchase support separately from post-purchase support so you can see whether it is moving checkout completion rather than just ticket volume.
caveats: The source states the principle ('a confused mind says no') but gives no staffing ratio, response-time target or tooling recommendation; set those from your own ticket data.
cards.source_name: How to Build an E-commerce Team from Scratch.docx

cards.title: Keep emotional engagement alive through fulfillment and packaging
cards.summary: Because people buy emotionally, fulfillment should protect that feeling with tracking codes, receipts and packaging worth the wait.
cards.use_when: Setting fulfillment team responsibilities and post-purchase experience standards, including packaging, tracking and delivery communication.
steps: Assign the fulfillment team explicit post-purchase responsibilities, not just picking and shipping: send a tracking code with a receipt so buyers can see where the order is.
Treat packaging as part of the product experience — make it look considered, because the unboxing is meant to justify the waiting time and sustain the emotion that drove the purchase.
Build a standard sequence: order confirmation, dispatch notice with tracking, and delivery follow-up, so customers are never left guessing during long transit times.
Review packaging cost against margin per order before upgrading materials; the source recommends quality packaging but gives no budget threshold.
Collect delivery complaints and repeat contact reasons and route them back to the fulfillment lead as fixable process failures.
Keep fulfillment standards documented so they hold when you add staff or use third-party logistics.
caveats: Packaging improvements are an opinion-backed practice here, not a tested result; weigh them against shipping cost and your actual margin.

cards.title: Build a digital marketing team that encodes your brand values
cards.summary: Marketing hires should understand company objectives and ethics, because buyers respond to brands whose values they can relate to.
cards.use_when: Writing the job spec for a media buyer or copywriter, or briefing campaign creative so ad messaging reflects the brand's actual positioning.
steps: State your mission and core values in the marketing brief, then require every sales message and campaign to represent them.
Use a concrete example as a standard: if you sell vegan products, express care for animals in the ad copy so value-aligned buyers resonate and buy.
Screen marketing candidates for whether they understand your objectives and ethics, not only for channel or platform skill.
Audit live ad copy against the values statement before scaling spend, and reject creative that contradicts the brand even if it performs.
Note that this is the source's stated opinion about brand-resonance advertising; treat the performance impact as untested and check it against your own ad data.
caveats: No campaign result or benchmark is provided for this approach; it is a positioning principle, and value-led copy can underperform pure direct-response creative.

cards.title: Treat the website as a leaky bucket and staff developers to plug drop-off
cards.summary: Every step of the site leaks leads and the developer/designer role exists to fix those leaks by simplifying navigation and checkout.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing drop-off on product pages and in the checkout flow, or justifying a web development or design hire.
steps: Frame the site as a leaky bucket: each interaction is a possible leak, and the developer/designer's job is to find and seal those pores.
Map the path from landing to checkout and list every step where a shopper can hesitate, get lost or abandon — pages, options, form fields, redirects.
Fix by simplifying: make the site quick to navigate and let shoppers jump straight to what they are looking for.
Do not display every product in one place; short attention spans mean an undifferentiated catalog loses money.
Deliver a smooth checkout: reduce friction in the purchase steps rather than adding choices, using the source's restaurant-hygiene analogy — nobody buys from a place that looks messy.
Assign one owner (developer or designer) to hold the leak-fixing roadmap so UX debt gets prioritised against new features.
caveats: This is an analogy and a principle, not a measured CRO process; pair it with your own funnel analytics to confirm which leaks actually cost the most.

cards.title: Sequence the five ecommerce roles before launch
cards.summary: A workable store needs five functional silos — administrator, customer service, fulfillment, digital marketing, and web development/design — and a founder can cover several at low budget.
cards.use_when: Planning your first hires or deciding which functions a small store can safely leave with the founder.
steps: List the five silos: administrator (strategy, contracts, partnerships, reporting, brand), customer service, order fulfillment, digital marketing, and web development/design.
Allocate each silo to a named owner, even if that owner is you; every unassigned silo becomes a launch blocker.
When budget is limited, cover the extra core tasks yourself rather than under-hiring a single generalist for all five.
Add people only as volume forces it — the source advises waiting until you are 'settled' rather than hiring for every seat up front.
Revisit the allocation when you scale payroll, checking whether the founder is still the bottleneck in any silo.
Keep the silo definitions written down so responsibilities do not blur as the team grows.
caveats: The source presents this as a starting template with no headcount-to-revenue ratios; adjust the sequencing to your order volume and channel mix.

cards.title: Screen candidates for drive, not just ability
cards.summary: A capable ecommerce team needs people who want to push to the next level, because you cannot get results from a bad team.
cards.use_when: Interviewing VAs, media buyers, operators or copywriters, or deciding whether a struggling team needs new people versus better process.
steps: Define the next-level goal you want the role to drive toward before the interview, so you can test whether the candidate is motivated by it.
Ask how the candidate has broken through a previous goal and what they changed to get there, looking for evidence of self-directed drive rather than assigned tasks.
Assess demonstrated role competence alongside process clarity, workload and tools; the source's emphasis on people quality does not prove every performance problem requires replacing people.
Combine drive with role-specific skill — enthusiasm does not substitute for administrative, service, fulfillment, marketing or development competence.
Document behavioural expectations for the role so new hires know what 'driving to the next level' looks like in daily work.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated belief, not tested evidence; 'drive' is hard to verify in interviews, so use past accomplishments rather than self-description.
